newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgaria opposition eyes victory amid gloom.
newsitem.headline: Bulgaria opposition eyes victory amid gloom.

text.p: Bulgarian voters, frustrated by a deep economic crisis and stalled reforms, look set to give anti-communist opposition candidate Petar Stoyanov a convincing win in Sunday's presidential election.
But the ruling Socialists, nervously awaiting talks with the International Monetary Fund on badly needed loans, insist that they alone can pull the impoverished Balkan country back from the brink.

A Gallup poll in the Trud daily predicted that Stoyanov, a liberal lawyer from the Union of Democratic Forces (UDF), would win 64 percent of votes cast against 36 percent for the Socialists' Ivan Marazov, who is Culture Minister.
The Centre for Analysis and Marketing gave Stoyanov 57 percent and Marazov 37 percent.
Under Bulgaria's post-communist constitution the president is a largely ceremonial figure and real power lies with parliament where Prime Minister Zhan Videnov's Socialists have a clear majority.
At a final rally on Friday night the Socialist treated elderly supporters to folk music and speeches evoking a lost communist era of cheap bread and safe streets.
"Turning to capitalism was a big mistake for Bulgaria. Everything was much better before (the 1989 fall of the communist regime)," pensioner Sultan Ignatov told Reuters.
But traders tending their stalls nearby did not see Marazov, a gentle, grey-haired art historian, as president.
"I am going to vote for Stoyanov as a protest against this government. I don't think Marazov deserves to be president," said Yordan Lyubomirov, in his 20s.

A big defeat for Marazov, who on Friday vowed to restore Bulgaria's communist-era close trade ties with Russia and other ex-Soviet states, could widen rifts in the Socialist Party and derail its shaky economic reforms, political analysts said.
In a televised debate on Thursday Stoyanov accused Videnov of making Bulgaria the laggard of East European reform.
"The most important question facing us now is simply survival through the coming winter," he said.

"Bulgarians don't know what to do tomorrow - they have to choose whether to buy bread or milk or to turn on the electricity. This is a very humiliating question at the end of the 20th Century," said the athletic, bespectacled Stoyanov.

Looming bread and fuel shortages and bank closures have thrown a dark shadow over an election campaign already marred by bombings and violence culminating in the October 2 assassination of former prime minister Andrei Lukanov.

Lukanov, a wealthy businessman and fierce critic of the government, was gunned down as he left his Sofia home. The lack of arrests in the case has reinforced Bulgarians' belief that the police are powerless to tackle the country's crime wave.
On Wednesday a member of the Central Electoral Committee, Haralambi Anchev, narrowly escaped assassination by a bomb which destroyed his car.
President Zhelyu Zhelev, also a liberal, dropped out of the election race after being defeated by Stoyanov in a June primary to select a single opposition candidate.
The head of an IMF mission arrived in Sofia on Friday for renewed talks on Bulgaria's heavy debt repayment schedule.
The central bank, hoping to convince the Fund of its commitment to reform, started bankruptcy procedures on Thursday against eight banks placed in receivership in September.
It also cut the annual interest rate to 180 percent from 240 percent.
